utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We will have the witness, who is being brought into court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies of course, and Mr. Djurdjic is now continuing with his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please open tab 21 in your binder. I would like to retrieve D008-4692. That would be 65 ter 1046. This is a note dated 19th of October, 1998 of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Mr. Jovanovic, this is a note on a meeting of Mr. Sainovic, deputy federal prime minister, and head of the UN mission for Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Staffan de Mistura. I would like to ask you to comment paragraph 2 under item 1 on page 1.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic, pointed out to the representative of the United Nations that segment of problems in Kosovo and Metohija which are result of involving civilians into the armed conflict as a result of the pressures exerted by the KLA organisation. Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic pays particular attention to the fact that the armed operations of the KLA which civilians getting involved in those give rise to displaced persons in Kosovo and Metohija in the opinion of Mr. Sainovic, and on the other hand, the Serb civilians are faced with the hostage crises and he also points out and highlights the abduction of a Tanjug reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would move to admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00472.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's see D008-4336.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 22 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic, and 65 ter document 984. Mr. Jovanovic, could you please briefly comment this document on how our diplomacy acted with respect to the establishment of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that two days after the signing of the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement, the OSCE sent to Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 2, if I may interrupt. Please do continue.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that the management of the OSCE two days after the signing of the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement sent a technical team to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order for them to perform certain preparatory actions in Kosovo and Metohija and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the deployment of the so-called Kosovo Verification Mission. And what is also evident in this official OSCE report, that the technical team of the OSCE was met with full co-operation, understanding of the both federal Yugoslav authorities, the republican Serbian authorities, and the local authorities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00473.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at D008-4698.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 23 and 65 ter 1047. This is a note dated 4th of November, 1998 on talks between the Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government, Mr. Sainovic, with the Austrian Ambassador, his excellence Mr. Petritsch held on the 3rd of November, 1998. Mr. Jovanovic, let's take a look at page 2 in English, please, and in Serbian that would be page 1, paragraph 2. It is stated here that Mr. Petritsch broached the issue of the further functioning of the EU's monitoring mission in Yugoslavia, that is, in Kosovo and Metohija. Could you comment -- respond to those requests, and what did the FRY do in respect of this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a note on the talks of Mr. Nikola Sainovic with the Austrian Ambassador Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch, and it is evident from this note that Sainovic briefed Mr. Petritsch on the creation of preconditions for the return of the displaced persons and to bring the situation back into normal, and he pin-points the need to do more to liberate the kidnapped Yugoslav journalists. With respect to Mr. Petritsch, he mainly agreed with such assessments, and what is important here is that he asked representative of the federal government for the ECMM, the European Commission Monitoring Mission, be allowed to work and to normalise its status in Kosovo and Metohija. Otherwise, ECMM had its headquarters in Bosnia-Herzegovina in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who headed KDOM of the European Union?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period until the withdrawal of the ECMM, the head of that mission in Kosovo and Metohija was a representative of the European Union from Germany, Mr. Dietmar Hartwig, and I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00474.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's take a look, please, at D010-5395. That would be 65 ter document 1791.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jovanovic, that would be tab 24 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've come to a document that we moved to be additionally added to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djurdjic, perhaps you can -- is it going to come up in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would be the first page in Serbian, and we're about to see page 2 in English. Now we're going back to page 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help me, Mr. Djurdjic. This is a correspondence in 2007. How is this relevant in our case and admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this letter is one that Mr. Hartwig, who used to be head of the KDOM of the European Union in 1998/1999 wrote to the then-Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, Madam Angela Merkel. And the letter contains his information and what he knew about the events in Kosovo and Metohija while he served there as the head of that mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see the name of Mr. Hartwig on your list of witnesses. Is it proposed to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig is not on our witness list, but this is a letter which was delivered to Witness Jovanovic, and Witness Jovanovic -- and this is from his personal archives and is familiar with this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you -- do you mean delivered to the witness in his capacity as minister? In his capacity -- in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hartwig and Mr. Jovanovic know each other personally from the time when Mr. Hartwig headed the KDOM of the EU in KiM, and after sending this letter he forwarded the letter to Mr. Jovanovic as can be seen on page 1 of the English version. It is seen here that this letter sent to the chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany is being forwarded to Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As we understand it, Mr. Jovanovic had been retired for some time in 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. After the letter was written, this copy was forwarded by Mr. Hartwig to Mr. Jovanovic. So this must have happened after the date of the letter, but it has been forwarded to Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I come then to my question: How is this admissible, this document? It's a letter not written by a witness. It is a letter sent to the head of state of another country. It is a letter that happens to be written by somebody who sent as a personal gesture a copy of it to the present witness, who was then an ordinary citizen living in retirement. Now, how is the contents of this letter going to be able to inform this Chamber anything about the facts of what occurred relevant to the indictment? It could be very different if Mr. Hartwig were to be a witness. We would certainly mark it for identification then if you saw fit, but if he's not to be called as a witness, what possible use can we make of this document in 2007 about events in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence holds that this document was delivered to Mr. Jovanovic by the author of the letter, and we believe that the contents of that letter are relevant for these proceedings. Unfortunately, Mr. Hartwig could not respond positively to the request of the Defence to testify in this trial. We did try, however, to secure him as a witness, and we believe that -- well, I don't know whether you are questioning the authenticity of this missive, and as to its contents I do believe that it is relevant for the period when the witness, as an actor in those events, was active. This is our proposal and our submission, and it's up to the Chamber to decide on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, may it please you. The Prosecution submits that the letter is inadmissible. I had prepared some written submissions on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in regard to a document of that nature to support the submission that it is inadmissible, but I think the issue has -- we have addressed the issue in a very direct way. This is a letter dated 2007 in which the person, the maker, relates what he perceived in 1998. It really amounts to a statement about his perceptions eight years before, and it is only admissible if it can satisfy one of the rules or one of the provisions of Rule 92 bis, or Rule 92 ter, or Rule 92 quater for admission of statements made by persons who do not testify. There is nothing before the Court which meets that foundation, and therefore it is not admissible. It may well be said that it might be squeezed in, so to speak, under the general provision of Rule 89(C), where the Court may use its discretion to admit any document which is relevant and probative. However, the submission in regard to that is that witness statements, as this document amounts to, falls clearly under Rules 92 bis, ter, and quater. Those rules being less lex specialis. And secondly, to satisfy Rule 89, it would have to be of some probative value, and it is the submission of the Prosecution that a statement of this nature of a witness who is speaking in 2007 about some events in 1999 could have no real probative value as to be admissible under Rule 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of the jurisprudence of this Chamber contradicts Mr. Stamp because we admitted a letter sent by Madam Louise Arbour to President Milutinovic, and Madam Arbour was not a witness in this trial either. This is P1511 in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the admission of that letter, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the purpose, I don't know. I think that this was admitted through a bar table motion, not through a witness. This was something I could find now doing a rush job --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are a variety of situations in which a letter may become admissible, but what we are dealing with here is a letter, the only relevance of which could be proof of the contents of the letter as representing the situation in 1998 and 1999. It's a letter that was not sent at that time to any official in the Government of Serbia. It was a letter sent some eight, nine years later to the head of the government of another country. And it happens that out of personal relationship, a copy came into the hands of Mr. Jovanovic. That doesn't lend any substance or verification to the truth and reliability of what is set out in the letter by the author of the letter. That's why I checked with you that it's not proposed by you to call as a witness the author of the letter. In the absence of that, I do not see how this document could properly be admitted into evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, had we been able to secure the presence of the witness we wanted to bring here very much Mr. Hartwig, then yes we would have tendered this letter into evidence through him, but due to his health condition, he was unable to come and testify for Defence. And given all the circumstances that you just enumerated, it is our position that you will be able best to assess the value of this -- probative value of this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, Mr. Djurdjic, the document, the letter, in 2007 is not admissible on any present basis for the purposes of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D008-4364.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 25, Mr. Jovanovic, for you. This is 991 Defence 65 ter document. Mr. Jovanovic, this is a report from a check-point dated 13th of November, 1998, outpost of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your comment -- but it seems that I have made a mistake. It should be page 2 in the English. Could you comment on item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see item 3 from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 3 they discuss the statement of the OSCE chairman, Mr. Geremek, who stated that he was concerned for further developments in Kosovo and Metohija and also estimated that March 1999 would be decisive for Kosovo and Metohija. And following that, you see the reaction of the Italian Ambassador, Mr. Sessa, who says that he did not understand such a statement of Mr. Geremek because one needed to look at the situation as it was without going into what was going to happen in March. This statement by Geremek could probably be dated to the first half of November when he said that March would be a crucial month for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00475.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-4368, 65 ter 992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 26 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is written communication between the outpost of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Pristina and the headquarters in Belgrade dated the 14th of November, 1998. In this letter they convey the request of the head of the KVM, Mr. Walker, to meet with the president of FRY on the 15th of November at 1500 hours in Belgrade. So this request is from the 14th, and the request was for Walker to be -- to meet with President Milosevic on the 15th at 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be interesting to have you explain to us who was the counterpart of Mr. Walker in him discharging his duties in Kosovo and Metohija. Who was his counterpart on the Yugoslav side and then who was his superior within the OSCE framework?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of normal, regular, diplomatic framework, Mr. Walker would communicate in Kosovo and Metohija with the head of the outpost of the foreign affairs ministry in Pristina and also high state officials who were located in Kosovo and Metohija. As for Belgrade, in accordance with the regular diplomatic practice, he would normally meet with the assistant minister of foreign affairs in charge of multi-lateral relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And as for Mr. Walker's superior, that was the chairman of the OSCE at the time foreign affairs of -- minister of Poland, Mr. Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00476.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D008-4380, which is 996 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your tab 27, Mr. Jovanovic. Briefly, please, can you tell me what steps were taken by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs -- just a moment, please. This is a note from the foreign affairs outpost in Kosovo and Metohija dated the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this note we can see what was done by the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to facilitate the work of the OSCE mission in Kosovo and Metohija and make it more efficient. You can see what elements of the government were involved in this effort to have the OSCE mission deployed as soon as possible and in order to have it operational as soon as possible. Let me just add that Ambassador Zoran Veljic who was in charge of these talks was prior to that and also later head of protocol within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00477.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D008-4372, please, 1048 on the 65 ter Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your tab 28, Mr. Jovanovic. This is a note from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from the 20th of November, 1998, and it deals with the talks between Mr. Sainovic and Bo Pellnas, head of the OSCE office in Belgrade. Could you please explain the first paragraph of this letter.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bo Pellnas was head of the OSCE liaison office with the government and authorities of Yugoslavia and Serbia in Belgrade. And in the absence of Ambassador Walker, head of the KVM, Mr. Sainovic lodged a protest with Mr. Pellnas in relation to the latest developments in Kosovo and Metohija, and he asked him to convey that protest to the leadership of OSCE in Vienna. Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic illustrated this situation, giving the reasons for lodging the protest, and the reasons were the killings and kidnapping of civilians of Albanian and Serbian ethnicity as well as constant attacks on policemen, which clearly represented huge losses and also endangered the political process. Sainovic also pointed out that a false balance was being established in various violations of accepted agreements and that law enforcement officials, state officials, were treated in the same way as terrorists who were attacking the state and its organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00478.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D1234, please, which is 504 on the 65 ter list of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is tab 29 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is official informative note of the foreign affairs outpost in Pristina on the talks between William Walker and the Army of Yugoslavia General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. This is quite a long document, so I will just ask for certain parts of it. Page 3 in English and page 2 in the Serbian version. Page 2, paragraph 2, somewhere in the middle. Could you please comment this portion.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loncar gave a proposal to Ambassador Walker as the head of the KVM mission to step-up verifications in the Pec, Pristina, Prizren, Podujevo, and some other places where there is an increased delivery of weapons from Albania and where also more intensive terrorist attacks were observed. He further points out that the terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija receive from abroad, mostly from Albania, standard weaponry plus some modern weaponry including rocket-launchers, black arrows, and similar systems. He further warns that such weapons delivery goes against the goals and objectives to which the Government of Yugoslavia and OSCE were committed. This is why it was in the joint interest to put an end to such activities, to put an end to further supply of weapons and other encouragement of terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija which was in accordance with the requests of the Security Council of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 4 in the English and page 3 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Under item 2, Mr. Kotur says something. Could you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur emphasized that co-operation with the KVM is ongoing and should be developing in accordance with the signed agreement on the establishment and the terms of reference of the KVM and that the Yugoslav side remains committed to consistent application of the signed agreement, nothing more or nothing less of what had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any requests at that time, and you may know of such on the part of the KVM, which surpassed the agreement or what was regulated by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such requests. I remember quite well that the bulk of the energy and the time was spent working on requests to enable the KVM to use their own aircraft, more specifically helicopters, and to allow the use, or rather, carrying of weapons for the security detail of the head of the mission in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to come to some documents which deal with that, but in the meantime I would like to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00479.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's take a look at document 65 ter 1236. That would be 507 on the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is a report dated 25th of December, 1998, coming from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs's outpost in Pristina concerning Mr. Sainovic's talks with Mr. Walker, head of the KVM. Let's see page 2 of the English version, please, and that would be page 1 on the Serbian. Please take a look at the segment just below the mid-point line discussing that he was -- he expressed regret about the co-operation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already stated, quite a number of meetings, quite a lot of energy and time were expended to meet the requests of the KVM which surpassed the framework of the agreement, and this document demonstrates that Mr. Nikola Sainovic expressed his regrets to Ambassador William Walker that the co-operation between the KVM and the competent Yugoslav and Serbian institutions was undergoing in the light and under the pressure on the basis of such unjustifiable requests such as the requests to use helicopters and to bear arms on the part of OSCE personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D00480.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's please see D004-0145. That would be 65 ter 1229 on the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 31 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. This is an outpost report on talks of deputy Federal Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic, with the Deputy Head of Mission, Mr. Keller, Ambassador Keller, which took place on the 6th of January, 1999, and the report is dated the 7th January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's please move to page 3 in English and page 2 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You see the beginning under the dash on the second page, the first sentence, could you please comment on the state of affairs during that period in Kosovo and Metohija at the time of these talks.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic informed French ambassador, Mr. Keller, deputy head of the KVM, on the detrimental effects to the general climate which were result of an explosive device being thrown at a cafe in Pristina, which resulted in deaths of several young men, Serbs. He demanded that the OSCE react more promptly and energetically, first and foremost in terms of them being faster to respond and to arrive to the crime scene whenever crimes were perpetrated against Serbian civilians or representatives of Serb authorities there. Furthermore, Mr. Sainovic highlighted the amassment of weapons and the fact that such weaponry is being modernised in the area of Podujevo, which is close to Albania. He also states that in other areas, such as the area of Pec and the area of Pristina, there were -- there was unrest there and that the consequences of weapons being amassed are that regular citizens are being more and more upset about the situation, uneasy, and that the conditions for political dialogues were being deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's going to Serbian page 3 and English page 4. Under item 2 you can see what Mr. Keller said. I would like to hear what you know about that, and if you could offer your comments. That would be sentence number three in that paragraph. The sentence is: "He confirmed that the departure of Serbs ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a consequence of more frequent terrorist actions, such as the placement of explosive devices in cafes, in other public places, there is more and more Serb civilians in Kosovo and Metohija who leave their settlements, and Mr. Keller characterised that as ethnic cleansing of the Serbs, and he was deputy head of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into evidence. Now let's take a look at D008 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00481.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at D008-4547. That would be Defence 65 ter document 1014.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And tab 32 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. Could you please explain what this document represents in terms of the functioning of your organs.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each visit of Yugoslav representatives abroad or to international organisations could have been effected only after the federal government or other institutions had adopted a platform for the Yugoslav delegation's work abroad. So -- and each such visit would be documented in the form of a note or a report on the talks held by the Yugoslav delegation with representatives of international organisations or foreign states. This is an information on the talks of the federal government's representatives with the European Commission officials and Belgian representatives. And this is just one of the activities of the foreign affairs ministry and the federal government and the conclusions of such and results of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00482.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's take a look at, please, D008-4495. That would be 1007 on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the visit of Sadako Ogata high Commissioner for Refugees of the UN. And that is dated, if we -- this is dated 6th of January, 1999. Let's take a look at page number 2 in English and page number 3 in Serbian. Just a second, please. Please focus on item 2 -- no, that's in English, page 2, that's okay. Item 2, Mr. Jovanovic, could you offer your comments, please, on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is evidence -- evident from this report on Madam Sadako Ogata's meeting is that Serbia sent several types of aid amounting to $150 million US to relieve the grave humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and that an additional 87 villages inhabited by both Serbs and others had been ethnically cleansed of Serbs, and those 87 villages had become exclusively Albanian. It is also said that openness of Yugoslavia and Serbia is reaffirmed for an immediate launch of political dialogue to at least reduce or put an end to terrorist attacks --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, that would be page -- next page in your binder in the Serbian version. What I'm referring to are pages in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Ogata, UN High Commissioner for Refugees, among others, visited Pec, Dragobilje, and Prizren. What is being stated is that the number of internally displaced persons had dropped significantly, that there was no humanitarian catastrophe. She pointed out that she had no objection with respect to the freedom and security of movement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00483.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we've seen several documents making reference to requests of the KVM to use helicopters and to carry personal weapons or side-arms. Was that in keeping with the agreement that you signed with Ambassador Mr. Geremek?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fell outside the scope of the agreement. The use of aircraft in the territory of any sovereign state is regulated exclusively by an express bilateral agreement or by provisions on that of some other agreements in terms of security aspects, et cetera. With respect to the side-arms, that also fell outside the scope of the agreement because the OSCE's mission was civilian and there was an express provision that -- to the effect that the federal government of Yugoslavia would be providing security and guaranteeing the security and safety of the verifying officers in its territory. Let us add that the federal government, since it was feeling constant pressure on the issue of the helicopters, offered to Mr. Walker Yugoslav civilian or other helicopters and Yugoslav airmen to be available 24/7 to Mr. Walker or to mission personnel for the purposes of verification. But despite repeated offers by the Yugoslav side, Mr. Walker, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, and others kept on insisting on using their own helicopters and using their side-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Who was authorised within the OSCE to request amendments to the agreement that was reached?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one of the signatories was authorised to do that in accordance with their internal procedures. So only OSCE or Yugoslavia could have done it in accordance with their internal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did OSCE ever launch such an initiative to amend the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was never done, either in writing or verbally such initiative was never launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-43 -- 4203.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is the foreign affairs ministry note dated the 5th of January, 1999, on the talks between Sainovic and Austrian President Heinz Fischer and minister of foreign affairs, Wolfgang Schussel. These talks were held in Vienna on the 4th of January, 1999. On the first page of this document, what do they say, what was the situation like? This is at the end of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment of the Government of Yugoslavia at the time was that the leadership of Kosovo Albanians did not accept political dialogue and that it wasn't just their position, as it seemed at first glance, but also that their position of refusing political dialogue was also something that was effected and that came into being under the influence of international political factors. In order to stabilise this and to facilitate political dialogue, Yugoslavia through bilateral contact attempted to secure a support from other European, American, and international partners for political dialogue. This is one of the visits illustrating this effort on the part of Yugoslavia to win support of important countries and important partners in order to exert some pressure on Albanian leadership, to accept political dialogue as the only avenue for reaching a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we, please, turn to the last page in your version, which is page 3 in the English version. And could you now, please, comment on this portion where Mr. Schussel says that on behalf of the EU he promises to do everything to bring to negotiations the Albanian side. So please tell us, what was the situation like when it comes to involving the Albanian side in negotiations, and what did Serbia do in order to secure their presence in order to reach a political settlement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of Kosovo Albanians practically sabotaged all efforts on the part of the Government of Serbia and Government of Yugoslavia to have the political dialogue commence unconditionally and without any further delay. The assessment was that Kosovo Albanians and their representatives were not interested in a compromise or in a political settlement that would be in accordance with the positions of the Security Council of the UN on sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and Serbia or in the essential autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija. They simply accepted the tactics of delay, the tactics of rejecting dialogue, awaiting a moment when somebody would bring them their statehood on a plate, if I may say so. This is a meeting, this is a dialogue, in which Austria, as a neighbour of Serbia and as an influential member of the European Union, undertook a certain kind of a diplomatic obligation to ensure the presence of Albanians at negotiations, to convince Albanians that it was in their interest to accept these urgent negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00484.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D008-4524, which is 1229 on Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is tab 36 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. We're interested in chronology. This is the basic position for the talks held by the federal government.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What position and what initiative will be put forward by the representatives of the Yugoslavia in their contacts with representatives of other countries and of international organisations was not a personal matter for them to decide upon personally, no. These issues were determined by the federal government, and their -- its representatives are duty-bound to use it in their contacts with representatives of foreign government in order to achieve the goals set by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D00485.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-4711, 1050 on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is your tab 35, Mr. Jovanovic. Briefly, please, this document is from the 21st of January. This is a letter sent by the federal government to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. You mentioned this in passing just now. This is binder 35, please -- tab 35 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a conclusion of the federal government which accepted the platform and the programme for the visit of a delegation headed by Sainovic to Sweden and Denmark from 18th to 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00486.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D228, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 37 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a protest note of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent to the OSCE mission in Kosovo and Metohija due to an incident at a border crossing caused by the OSCE representatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. We can read that. I'm interested in this: So this was a protest that was formally lodged in writing. Have you ever received any protest from KVM or OSCE in relation to the agreement on verification during their stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never received such protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to a different topic, namely, Rambouillet negotiations. Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering this last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's already in evidence in our case, D228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you personally participate in Rambouillet negotiations, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time I was not in Rambouillet, and incidentally there were no negotiations held there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, how was the delegation of the FRY and Serbia set up for Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joint Yugoslav-Serbian delegation that was set up by the Government of Serbia and Government of Yugoslavia. It was headed by Deputy Prime Minister of Serbia, Professor Ratko Markovic, and the delegation comprised officials mostly from Serbian authorities. As for the representatives of the federal government, there were two deputy prime ministers of the federal government, Professor Kutlesic and Professor Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovanovic, can you tell us, please, do you know what were -- what was the mandate of our delegation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Yugoslav-Serbian delegation had a mandate to negotiate directly with the representatives of the Albanian national minority in order to achieve a compromise, a political and peaceful settlement which would be based on the resolutions of the UN Security Council and the agreement, final act of the OSCE, and which would be based on the right to equality of all ethnic communities and all citizens in Kosovo and Metohija. These solutions were to represent the broadest autonomy of Kosovo within the framework of Serbia and based on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see D008-2666.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 38 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. This is a statement of our delegation. This is D004-2666. So this is a statement of our delegation from the 11th of February, 1999. I'm interested in paragraph 1, where it says: "The delegation accepts the following general elements set by the Contact Group ..." Tell me, please, were these ten principles of the Contact Group negotiable, could they negotiate on it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not negotiable. The Serbian and Yugoslav delegation faced a boycott of the negotiations in Rambouillet. These negotiations simply failed to commence, and in order to jump-start negotiations and to make a breakthrough in the stalemate, our delegation proposed that the two delegations signed to these basic principles set by the Contact Group and to use this as a basis to commence negotiations in order to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00487.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you told us that you did not personally participate in these negotiations. Could you tell me what was the role of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in organising these negotiations and implementing them. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs provided technical and administrative logistics for negotiations, but as I have mentioned to you they were no negotiations because there were no direct dialogues between the two relevant delegations. There are some perceptions present that an agreement was reached in Rambouillet. An agreement presupposes some sort of an accord between the two sides. There was no accord, which means there was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have some further documents to look at and to comment upon, but please tell me this: In this mediation that took place, was there any effort to link up political agreement and implementation with the bringing in of foreign troops in the territory of Serbia and Yugoslavia, and was this something that they negotiated upon and reached an agreement on?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to events in Rambouillet, this was a very peculiar form of shuttle diplomacy under one roof. The two delegations that came to negotiate there did not in fact negotiate; rather, the so-called international negotiators, Mr. Chris Hill, US ambassador; Mr. Petritsch, the Austrian ambassador; and a representative of the European Union; as well as Mr. Mayorski, the Russian Federation ambassador, served as mediators or facilitators between the two delegations staying in the same palace. There was no possibility of a breakthrough there of achieving some progress because the two delegations never actually met. However, the tactics of the two out of three international negotiators was to distribute the text of the so-called agreement to the Serbian delegation, to feed it to them in small doses, to spoon-feed it to them. So the Serbian delegation, in fact, never received the entire proposal or the entire draft agreement, so-called agreement. No. It was given to them in small doses, bit by bit. What was particularly peculiar was that the two international negotiators practically concealed, until the very end, their texts which pertained to the military presence and the military components of international forces in Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, in the territory of entire Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now take a look at D008-4567. That would be 1018 on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Jovanovic, that would be tab 39. Let's not waste time. Please tell us, is this usual method of reporting, and it concerns report on the visit of Greek minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Pangalos on the 10th and 11th [as interpreted] of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the usual way of briefing the government on the results of each international visit received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00488.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's take a look at D008-4589. That would be 1020 on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 40, Mr. Jovanovic. These are positions of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs submitted to the president of the federal government, Momir Bulatovic on the 19th of February, 1999. Could you please tell us the reasons for drafting those positions and to explain those positions briefly, why they were adopted and how?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-February 1999, public speculation abounded on military presence by NATO forces in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a result of the Rambouillet agreement. Even some alleged accords from Rambouillet were being published in daily newspapers in Albanian in Kosovo and Metohija. And those texts contained solutions or proposals for a military presence of NATO in the territory of Yugoslavia. To curb such speculations and to explain the position of Yugoslavia against the deployment of NATO forces throughout its territory, the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs drafted those positions and the federal government adopted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00489.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's please take a look at document 1280 on our 65 ter list and that would be 4001 on Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that would be tab 41 in your binder. Mr. Jovanovic, please explain what this document is, and this is a letter dated the 5th of March, 1999, by the President of Serbia, Milutinovic, and the Deputy Prime Minister Markovic. I would like you to comment paragraph 3 which starts with the words "unfortunately," with respect to those alleged agreements.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As has been noted the head of the Serbian and Yugoslav delegation was Professor Ratko Markovic, vice-president of the Serbian government, but during the delegation's stay at Rambouillet, if I remember correctly, President of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, visited that delegation on two or three occasions. After such a visit, after an assessment had been made that the Albanian side influenced or in concert with certain influential countries is sabotaging talks at Rambouillet, President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, decided to warn ministers of foreign affairs of the Contact Group of such things in writing, first and foremost he addressed the three -- the troika which managed the negotiations, which would be ministers of foreign affairs of the US, the UK, and France. And this letter is the one that President of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, sent to those ministers warning them that the Albanian side was spreading news and speculations, rumours, that the agreement had been reached and that was about to be signed in the shortest possible time. Paragraph 3 on page 1 confirms that chapters 2, 5, and 7 regulating the military component and military presence of NATO in the territory of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been hidden away and not disclosed and that the tactics at play boiled down to public pressure being exerted against the Serbian side to accept those chapters which it had not been informed upon at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00490.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at D008-4593. That would be 1021 on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 42 in your binder. This would be a report on your talks with Mr. Joschka Fischer, German foreign affairs minister, submitted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to the federal government, talks were conducted on the 8th of March, 1999, in Germany. Please turn to page 3, Mr. Jovanovic, of that agreement. That would be page 7 in e-court. Please comment this paragraph: "On behalf of the EU and the Contact Group," that would be paragraph 1 on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: European Union and the Contact Group through an influential member, which Federal Republic of Germany was, confirmed that they were continually committed to peace in Kosovo, but also for Kosovo and Metohija to remain within the boundaries of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, within the boundaries of Serbia. They advocated an opinion that the military presence was necessary. I personally and my side on that occasion handed over a written aide-memoire, it was a document, that I handed over to Mr. Joschka Fischer, foreign minister of the Federal Republic of Germany, entitled The Activities of Separatists and Terrorists From Within the Territory of the Federal Republic of Germany. This document contained very specific and precise events and activities which were illegal activities, launched from the territory of Germany aimed at destabilising Serbia and Yugoslavia and to destabilise Kosovo and Metohija through the funding, arming, and training of the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00491.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we are past the time for our break. I have -- I need five minutes to admit two documents after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break and you can be sure that you have not overlooked anything, and we will finish in the few minutes after we resume. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. We resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness comes in, may I avail myself of this opportunity to say this. You instructed us yesterday to have this document MFI'd from French into English. We've done that. We've requested a translation, and we've repeatedly received an answer that there is no translation from one official language of this Court to another official language of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber wishes to do so, the Defence will take it upon themselves to have the document translated. It would be no problem for us, an authorised translation, not a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will not step on the corns of authority, Mr. Djurdjic. We will read the document for ourselves in French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is a pot of money available to us, and we can make use of it to fund this translation into English. That would be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, don't bother. Keep the pot of money for more useful purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let's take a look at document D008-4612. That would be 1022 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And tab 43 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. These are minutes of the 52nd meeting of the federal government, dated the 19th of March, 1999, and it is evident from the minutes that you attended that meeting and makes reference to an information that you provided on the talks about the Kosovo and Metohija situation at Rambouillet, Paris. So please briefly tell us something about your report and what was the main point thereof.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of that report which I submitted to the federal government is that the Serbian-Yugoslav delegation departed for Rambouillet and Paris to achieve a peaceful political solution for Kosovo and Metohija, but that the negotiations or, in other words, the meetings or activities were discontinued against the wish of the Serbian and Yugoslav delegation. Here in my report what is laid down are an understanding of the reasons why no negotiations practically took -- had taken place in Rambouillet, and there is a section of the report on the withdrawal of the KVM from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. An important assessment is contained therein to the effect that the end of the meetings at Rambouillet and Paris were a result of developments which could not be ascribed in any way to Serbia and Yugoslavia and that those hinder the achievement of a political solution. And on the other hand, those represented enormous public endorsement of separatism and terrorism of the KLA in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go to page 2. That would be page 5 in e-court in the English version. Mr. Jovanovic, please comment item 3.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item makes reference or is -- has to be construed in the light of the so-called Act. Order, an unveiled threat against Yugoslavia because of the Serbian-Yugoslav delegation is now being blamed for failure to accept -- or that it has tried to dispute the Rambouillet agreements. I have to highlight the fact that no agreement was reached at Rambouillet or Paris. There were no negotiations. There was not a single working meeting of the two delegations, and I would like to say that the international mediators were continually hiding the key elements of the agreement from the Serbian-Yugoslav delegation, those which concerned the deployment of NATO forces throughout the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here and ask you about this Annex B in the chapters 2, 5, and 7 of the implementation of the alleged agreement. What that annex referred to and what kind of powers did it bestow upon NATO?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chapters 2, 5, and 7 were virtually expressly empowered NATO to occupy the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Let me cite you, if you allow me, Your Honours, two or three illustrations concerning that alleged agreement from Rambouillet. One is that NATO is given the right to carry out manoeuvres, to bivouac, to transit through the territory, to use all transport communications and infrastructure for waterways, air traffic, road traffic, and railway traffic without seeking prior consent from the Serbian or Yugoslav authorities and without any compensation for possible damage resulting from the manoeuvres, exercises, or the presence of NATO troops in the territory. The second provision was that members of NATO or so-called international military forces would be entitled to put behind bars any citizen of Serbia or Federal Republic of Yugoslavia without any consent, any decision by competent authorities, and that provision makes reference only to the following situation. Shortly after an arbitrary arrest of a Yugoslav citizen, NATO would hand such persons over to the competent authorities. Such a provision entitling members or representatives of foreign countries in the territory of federal Yugoslavia to more rights than enjoyed by the domestic population is what can be deemed or termed capitulation in international legal framework. The third provision was that international military forces or NATO in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be expressly entitled to take over and manage for an unlimited period of time of the overall electro-magnetic spectrum in Yugoslavia, which practically means that without prior announcement or without seeking anybody's approval or consent to use the installations of civilian TV, civilian radio network without limitation in time or space, to use the frequencies of the Ministry of the Interior, of the military, of the health system, of the utility companies. So the entire electro-magnetic spectrum of the country, which is a national resource, may be taken by NATO without prior announcement, without seeking consent, without any limitations in space or time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just very briefly, item 4, the penultimate and ultimate sentence, namely that the negotiations are being postponed if FRY declared that they will not accept the agreements.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a contradiction. The first part says that the talks are being postponed, and the second part says that the talks would not continue unless - and this is a very interesting provision - because they say the "Serbs," not Serbia or Yugoslavia, so unless the Serbs declare that they accept the agreements. So this is effectively an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00492.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-43629 -- 4629, which is 1029 on the Defence list. Could we see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We have conclusions of the federal government from the 19th of March. Let me just repeat the number, D008-4629, 1025 on our 65 ter list, which is your tab 44. Item 1 of the conclusions. Were you informed about the evacuation of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The agreement was signed jointly by the OSCE and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is an international legal document which was implemented by Yugoslavia bona fide. So even though the agreement was an expression of accord between the two sides, we see here in this provision that this agreement was signed unilaterally without even notifying the other signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please comment on item 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the position of the federal government that it would protect the OSCE property in its territory in accordance with the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the FRY and Serbia ensure safe withdrawal of the KVM from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia ensured all conditions and all -- provided all safety measures for the work of the KVM and ensured that they could withdraw without any hindrance, which is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we receive it, Mr. Djurdjic, the witness may be able to help the Chamber. This purports to be conclusions reached by the federal government at a meeting, yet the report does not give the date of the meeting. It seems to be something that is prepared in anticipation. It's a session held on blank March 1999. Could you assist the Chamber with that, please, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is hard now to remember all the details, especially concrete dates, but knowing the situation at the time and the urgency of everything that was happening I think that this meeting was held either at the 19 -- either on the 19th or 20th at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, if I can assist, would you please look at the first page. There is a stamp there. Can you see a date there? Perhaps that could assist us.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy is illegible in the part where the date is and it's hard for me to see it. However, Your Honour, there is no doubt, if I may, that this draft of conclusions or this proposal for conclusions was sent to the federal government, as it says in the introductory portion on the 19th of March, most likely, 1999; and that the government received the draft which is certified by the received stamp on the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00493.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-4783, 1058 on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, during the aggression against the FRY, were there any attempts, and what do you know about efforts to maintain contact with representatives of the Albanian political parties which had not been engaged in terrorism?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though the war was on, the federal government and the Republic of Serbia did not abandon their efforts to achieve a peaceful political settlement with the representatives of Albanian minority in Kosovo and Metohija on the basis of compromise and abiding by all the principles of the Security Council. This information on the talks held between Nikola Sainovic, Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government; and the political leader representing the moderate political option in Kosovo and Metohija, Ibrahim Rugova, is yet another illustration of these constant efforts by the Government of Yugoslavia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, this is a joint communique following the meeting held in Pristina between deputy Federal Prime Minister, Sainovic, and Dr. Ibrahim Rugova from the 5th of April, 1999. I tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00494.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D002-1730, 1251 on the 65 ter list of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a joint communique of the federal government and Serbian government from the 6th of April, 1999. Just very briefly, Mr. Jovanovic, what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This joint communique, even though it was joint, had been adopted at the separate sessions of the federal government and Serbian government. It was previously harmonised between the two governments, and this reflects the constitutional relations between two subjects of the Yugoslav Federation in accordance with the constitution. This communique is yet another example of efforts made during NATO aggression as well aimed at finding a peaceful political settlement. And at finding an agreement with the representatives of the moderate factions, among whom was Ibrahim Rugova, yet again trying to reduce tensions and find a peaceful political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we know its date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I said that it was on the 6th of April, 1999. That's the last page of the document, if we can turn to that page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00495.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, thank you for responding to the invitation of the Defence to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, thank you for allowing us to conclude our examination-in-chief. I have no further questions for Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. We will wait a few moments while a technical problem with the transcript is dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am told the technical problem is affecting other courtrooms as well, so we will wait a few moments in the hope that it will be corrected. We are advised it may be some five minutes or so. The Chamber will rise temporarily and return as soon as the equipment is functioning again. --- Break taken at 4.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony here today you spoke about some United Nations Security Council Resolutions, and it seemed that you're advocating that they ought to be respected and complied with. Is that your position, that the United Nations resolutions ought to be respected and complied with?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One of them that you referred to specifically was Security Council Resolution 1199 of September 1998, and that is D160. And could we go straight to paragraph 13 in both the English and the B/C/S. You see that paragraph calling upon the authorities of the FRY, among others, to co-operate fully with the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your -- well, I could take it that your position is that this provision ought to be respected and complied with?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The resolution -- according to the resolution of the Security Council, all decisions need to be implemented in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a speech on the occasion of the 11th anniversary of the Socialist Party of Serbia in July 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details. At the time there were numerous speeches that I held, there were numerous occasions when I gave statements. And despite all my efforts, I'm unable to remember that particular speech from July that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But in July 2001 you recall that you were the president or acting president of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For some time I was acting chairman of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 06021. This is taken from the official ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, asks that we see a document which was put on the list after the witness started his evidence, or rather, after the Defence was banned from having any communication with the witness. So the witness is completely unaware of this document. And as for this first document, I don't think we even have the Serbian translation, this particular document that Mr. Stamp has just announced. So we received in the night between Sunday and Monday some two documents, and then yesterday while Mr. Jovanovic was testifying and today we received two documents as well. I have no objections to Mr. Stamp putting questions to Mr. Jovanovic in this manner, but putting such documents to the witness, especially untranslated documents, I think is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Clearly, untranslated documents are not usually convenient or fair. We will see whether the witness has difficulty understanding the document; and if that is the case and that can't be overcome by oral quotation from it in the course of the hearing, we will have to make some other arrangements. But for the moment, please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you read and speak English?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The speeches including -- or in particular speeches delivered by yourself as acting president of the SPS, the Socialist Party of Serbia, were published on the official web site of the party. You recall that was the practice in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No matter how I try, I cannot give you an affirmative answer to that question because to tell you the truth, I never followed web sites. Now, even though everything is hardly legible, very small font, I have to tell you that this is not an official document, either an official political or state document, nor is it an official SPS document. And please look at what's written under the heading. It's a document of a certain Miroslav Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. -- very well, very well --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And understandably, I do not want to be drawn into commenting on the documents which do not have a clear provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jovanovic. This document, I represent to you, was taken from the official web site of your party, and I want you -- and it purports to be a record of a speech you gave on that day. And I'd like to show you a part of it and ask you if you recall making those statements.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, would you please take a note of the fact that this is a private document of Mr. Miroslav Antic, who I'm totally unfamiliar with, either as a member of the SPS or either as a member of the diplomatic corps. I simply do not know this person. I do not think it would be fair from you to attempt to draw me into commenting upon the content of the document, whose character and provenance are not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend, Mr. Stamp, insists for the second time that this is a document of the Socialist Party of Serbia. I would kindly ask him to point us to a place in the document where this can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, I suggest, is not going to be a useful use of our time. The course Mr. Stamp proposed is a proper and usual one, to see whether the witness recalls saying words that are quoted in this document. If he does, there will obviously be some questioning following; if he does not, the matter comes to an end for the moment. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could look at page 8 of the -- of this document. Perhaps we could just go to the last two lines of page 7 and then return to page 8. And if it could be -- if we could pan in a little bit. And then if we could move to page 8 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In reference to Slobodan Milosevic and the fact that he was sent here for trial, this records you as saying that: " ... the so-called trial they are preparing, whose farcical beginning indicates how it will proceed, cannot fool most people. Virtually all Serbian people and a vast part of the real international community knows that this stage-managed affair aims to justify the crimes of NATO's leaders, especially the leaders of the former American administration, crimes against peace and humanity."
